cultivar: Jin Mu Dan (Tieguanyin × Huang Dan hybrid, 220)
processing: Medium-light oxidation with gentle shaking to build aroma, strip-rolled and lightly to medium charcoal roasted; the same cultivar is also widely made into black tea.
harvest_season: Spring, an early sprouter picked from mid to late April, as mature shoots with three or four open leaves.
appearance_dry: Tight, slim dark olive-brown strips with a strong sweet, flowery smell.
appearance_wet: Soft, medium-sized yellow-green leaves with thin red edges.
taste_profile: Peony and gardenia florals with honey and ripe fruit (apricot, lychee), a sweet, smooth, medium-light body and a soft toast underneath; the finish is clean rather than mineral.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, porcelain gaiwan, short steeps. It is at its most fragrant in the first three infusions; lengthen gradually after that and stop when it turns watery.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, lightly roasted and typically on sale from summer with the year stated. Like the other aromatic hybrids it is a drink-young tea: best within a year or two of harvest, kept sealed, and not a candidate for ageing.
description:
Jin Mu Dan, the golden peony, is one of the family of aromatic hybrids that the Fujian Tea Research Institute bred from Tieguanyin and Huang Dan, alongside Jin Guan Yin and Huang Guan Yin. It is the fruitiest of the three, and in Wuyi it makes a sweet, flowery, inexpensive rock tea that converts people who think they dislike roasted oolong.

The cross dates from the late 1970s, and the cultivar was selected over the following two decades and registered in the 2000s under the trade number 220. It sprouts early, grows vigorously and yields well, and it carries an unusual amount of aroma precursors in the leaf, which is why it was quickly taken up for several styles: strip-rolled yancha in Wuyi, ball-rolled oolong in Minnan, and especially black tea, where it makes a honeyed, floral cup.

As yancha it is picked in the second half of April, before the classic Wuyi cultivars, oxidised to a medium-light level and given a light to medium charcoal roast. The restraint is deliberate: the appeal is peony, gardenia, ripe apricot and honey, and a heavy roast would cook all of that off. The body is medium-light and smooth, with a gentle toastiness, and the finish is clean and sweet rather than stony.

Brew it hot and short in a gaiwan; it gives three brilliant steeps and three or four decent ones. It is a natural first tea of a session or a tea for the afternoon with something sweet.

It is sold by the current spring harvest and should be drunk within a year or two. It is cheap enough to find its way into aromatic Da Hong Pao blends and into flavoured-tea-sounding products that are in fact just Jin Mu Dan, so if a Wuyi tea smells improbably of flowers and fruit, this cultivar is usually the reason rather than any added flavouring. If you like it, the black tea made from the same leaf is worth a detour.
sources_note: Parentage (Tieguanyin × Huang Dan) and trade number 220 from Chinese cultivar lists; registration dates vary between provincial (2003) and national (2010) listings and are given here only as the 2000s.
history:
Jin Mu Dan is a modern bred cultivar, not an old Wuyi bush. Chinese cultivar lists give its parentage as Tieguanyin crossed with Huang Dan, the plant behind Huang Jin Gui, and it is listed as a national cultivar.

Its aroma has made it useful to breeders as well: Chinese trials have used it as a mother plant to select further fragrant lines. The same work records its weak points, poor tolerance of thin soil, early ageing and low resistance to stress.
